Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) said Wednesday that humanoid robots could become a major driver of memory and storage demand in the years ahead, a shift analyst Shay Boloor believes would be the turning point for physical AI demand.

MU’s Humanoid Memory Forecast

On Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said autonomous vehicles are the first big use case for physical AI, requiring more than 200 gigabytes of memory and multiple terabytes of storage.

That shift, he said, is expected to extend to humanoid robots and other autonomous systems.

“Physical AI can become a significant driver of memory and storage demand by the end of this decade,” Mehrotra said, adding that several physical AI customers are already sampling Micron’s next-generation products.

The chipmaker is increasing investment in its technology roadmap to ensure it is prepared to capitalize on this opportunity.

The company expects first-half capital expenditure of around $25 billion after reporting $10.8 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter.

Read Also: Trump Says Jerome Powell Should 'Resign' or Be 'Sued' Over Fed Renovation Failures — Watchdog Report Finds No 'Criminal' Wrongdoing

Beyond the Data Center

Futurum Equities‘ chief market strategist Boloor, on X said the shift would effectively put “server level memory into millions of machines outside the data center.”

Tesla Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:TSLA) Optimus is built around the ambition of a general-purpose humanoid that can handle a wide range of physical tasks, while XPeng Inc. (NYSE:XPEV) has launched an automated production line for its own IRON humanoid robot.

Micron’s Record Quarter

Micron posted fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, beating analyst estimates of $50.75 billion, according to Benzinga Pro.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $33.42 per share, topping estimates of $31.45.

For the first quarter, Micron expects revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, above estimates of $56.55 billion, and adjusted earnings of $37.15 to $39.15 per share, versus estimates of $35.07.

On Wednesday, Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) has signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy Corp. (NASDAQ:CEG) to secure nuclear power from Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs plant, as surging AI demand pushes technology companies to seek reliable electricity.

Amazon Locks In 690 MW From Maryland Nuclear Plant

Under the agreement, Amazon will purchase 690 megawatts of power from Calvert Cliffs, a 1,790-MW nuclear facility and Maryland’s only nuclear power plant.

The deal is expected to support more than $3 billion in infrastructure investment in Maryland, including about 190 MW of new emissions-free generating capacity expected to come online between 2030 and 2032.

"This agreement demonstrates how private investment can strengthen critical energy infrastructure," said Constellation CEO Joseph Dominguez.

Amazon and Constellation also entered a separate retail electricity supply agreement covering Amazon’s operations across the 13-state PJM power market.

Read Also: Amazon Signs $1 Billion Synopsys Deal as AWS Steps Up Nvidia Challenge

Amazon Deal Could Extend Calvert Cliffs Operations

Amazon’s long-term commitment is also expected to support Constellation’s efforts to renew Calvert Cliffs’ operating license for another 20 years.

Calvert Cliffs currently supplies about 80% of Maryland’s clean electricity, according to the companies. Its two reactors generate enough electricity to power more than 1.3 million homes.

AI Power Demand Drives Nuclear Investment

Market commentator the Kobeissi Letter estimates global electricity demand from AI could surge more than 1,100% by 2033 to about 315 gigawatts, with the U.S. accounting for roughly 200 gigawatts of the increase.

AI data centers are also putting additional pressure on power infrastructure during model training, when large numbers of GPUs operate simultaneously.

That synchronized demand can spike electricity consumption by as much as 50% above a facility’s designed capacity.

Nuclear plants can provide continuous electricity without direct carbon emissions during generation, making them an increasingly attractive option.

Last week, Southern Company’s (NYSE:SO) Georgia Power and Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google announced an agreement to support nuclear power uprates at the Vogtle and Hatch plants.

The aim is to increase clean electricity supplies for Google’s data centers.

In January, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (NYSE:BABA) also entered into a nuclear power partnership in China.

Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) have also made nuclear power agreements to secure electricity for their energy-intensive data centers.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) criticized President Donald Trump’s approach to artificial intelligence, warning that limited federal oversight could leave the rapidly evolving technology without sufficient safeguards.

Newsom Slams Trump’s AI Approach

On Wednesday, Newsom made the remarks in a post on X while sharing a clip of himself discussing AI regulation.

"What we saw from the White House yesterday was bullshit," he wrote. "It’s like Big Pharma saying we don’t need the FDA. Donald Trump’s ‘let it rip’ approach to AI is RECKLESS."

In the clip, Newsom compared AI oversight to regulations governing pharmaceuticals and airlines, arguing that industries should not be left to determine on their own whether government safeguards are necessary.

"What I heard in Washington, D.C., yesterday was bullshit. That should scare the hell out of everybody," he said.

He argued that California must continue strengthening its AI regulations in the absence of stronger federal leadership.

"We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership, which they doubled down on yesterday," Newsom said. "And so it only reinforces the imperative for us to accelerate our timelines."

Newsom said an independent group established through his executive order would review AI-related issues, with California planning to implement its recommendations once the review is complete.

Newsom Highlights AI Accord Typo

Newsom shared the White House’s announcement of the "Accord on Super Intelligence" on X, captioning it "The Golden Age of Super Intelligence."

The image he shared highlighted a spelling error in the document, which referred to the "United States" as "Unites States" beneath Trump’s signature.

Read Also: Trump Rejects Deeper AI Cooperation With China, Says It Could Mean Giving Away ‘Lot Of Secrets’ — ‘Whoever Wins Super Intelligence Wins’

Trump Unveiled AI Safety Pact

On Tuesday, Trump brought leaders of major AI companies together around a voluntary safety pact that called for independent audits, stronger internal controls and board-level oversight of advanced AI systems.

Trump released the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, also called a "Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities," after hosting technology executives at the White House.

The agreement was signed by Trump and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOG) CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang.

Trump described the pact as "morally binding" and said companies should take responsibility for policing their own AI development.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) criticized President Donald Trump’s new voluntary artificial-intelligence safety pact Wednesday, calling the agreement "entirely unenforceable" and arguing that industry self-regulation will not adequately protect Americans.

Jeffries Rejects Voluntary AI Self-Regulation

"The notion of entering into a voluntary agreement that is entirely unenforceable, and that allows the industry writ large to police itself, is not the right response at this moment," Jeffries told reporters according to The Hill. He cited warnings from AI developers and recent episodes in which autonomous agents acted outside their intended scope.

Trump unveiled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence on Tuesday after meeting executives from Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG), Anthropic, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA). He described the pact as "morally binding" and "almost like a constitution." The agreement is not legally binding, but calls for stronger internal controls, independent outside audits and board-level oversight of advanced models.

Read Also: Trump Rejects Deeper AI Cooperation With China, Says It Could Mean Giving Away ‘Lot Of Secrets’ — ‘Whoever Wins Super Intelligence Wins’

Trump Defends Industry-Led Safety Approach

Trump has framed industry self-regulation as a way to address AI safety concerns without slowing U.S. technological development. He has repeatedly resisted broader limits that could slow development, while House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has similarly argued against an AI moratorium.

Rogue Agent Incidents Fuel Safety Debate

Jeffries said recent incidents show why Congress should move faster. OpenAI disclosed in July that an autonomous agent escaped a controlled testing environment and breached Hugging Face, an episode Reuters described as "unprecedented." OpenAI has since investigated additional unauthorized activity, including agents accessing government websites, and recently paused training on newer models while strengthening safeguards.

"We’ve now seen multiple examples, some very extraordinary, like the Hugging Face incident, where AI agents have gone rogue," Jeffries said, adding that Congress should act "not in the next Congress, but right now."

The dispute comes as public concern rises. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released last month found 73% of Americans believed AI companies were not doing enough to prevent serious harm.

Trump’s accord leaves the door open to future rules, while Jeffries and other Democrats argue voluntary commitments do not provide enough accountability. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) separately dismissed the pact as "pinky promises."

Bets on Growth Above 3.3%

Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Muse AI agent is facing fresh privacy and safety questions after reports emerged of unexpected access to private messages and sensitive user information.

Elon Musk Amplifies Muse Privacy Concerns

On Sunday, Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) CEO Elon Musk reposted a post from Gizmodo Senior Editor Ray Wong, who criticized Muse after sharing an account in which the AI agent allegedly provided a Facebook Marketplace seller with a user’s address, resulting in sellers showing up at the person’s home.

Musk heads SpaceX, which offers rival AI services and the Grok chatbot.

Wong called the incident "dangerous and creepy," adding, "This would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman."

Wong also shared an Inc. report titled "Meta’s New Muse AI Agent Read My Private Messages. I Never Asked It To," raising additional questions about the agent’s access to sensitive information.

Read Also: Meta Pulls AI Image Feature After Privacy Backlash, Admits It 'Missed the Mark' Amid SAG-AFTRA Criticism

Meta Defends Muse’s Privacy Controls

Meta Superintelligence Labs executive David Singleton responded to the Inc. report on Threads, saying the company takes reports of potential security issues seriously.

Singleton said Muse’s Messages integration on Mac is optional and requires users to enable the Messages connector and grant Muse Full Disk Access through macOS.

He noted that users must go through multiple application and system-level permission steps before Muse can access Messages content.

According to Singleton, those protections are designed to prevent Muse from bypassing permissions even if the application itself contains a bug. He also said Full Disk Access can be disabled by users.

In response to Benzinga’s request for comment, Meta cited Singleton’s response to Wong’s post on X. Singleton said, "In the past, when we’ve worked with users to investigate similar reports, we’ve consistently learned that Muse was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission. Would love to help and figure out what’s going on hokaere."

Muse AI Agent Can Act On Users’ Behalf

Meta describes Muse as a personal AI agent designed to interact with a user’s digital life. Its capabilities include shopping, accessing connected applications and completing tasks on a user’s behalf.

In an earlier blog post, Meta said the tech giant "built Muse from the ground up to be a safe, secure, private, and widely available personal AI agent."

The backlash also comes at a time when reports about AI agents from OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google going rogue have also heightened concerns.

On Wednesday, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) criticized President Donald Trump’s approach to AI regulation, questioning whether the technology’s richest and most influential leaders should be trusted to police an industry that could generate enormous fortunes.

Sanders Challenges Trump On AI Guardrails

Sanders took aim at Trump in a post on X after the president unveiled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The senator shared a clip of Trump speaking to reporters about AI guardrails after the White House luncheon with technology executives. A reporter asked Trump why the public shouldn’t be concerned about AI and why the technology shouldn’t have guardrails.

"Because we have people that love our country and love the world a lot," Trump said.

When the reporter responded that AI safety requires more than love, Trump pointed to his head and said the people involved are "the smartest people in the world."

Sanders subsequently questioned that reasoning, arguing that relying on AI leaders to regulate themselves creates a potential conflict because many of them stand to benefit financially from the technology.

"You’re asking us to trust the people who stand to make trillions from AI to regulate themselves?" Sanders wrote.

Read Also: Bernie Sanders Slams Mike Johnson Over ‘Chinese Psyop’ Allegation on Opposition to Data Centers: ‘Americans Have Not Fallen Victim’

Sanders Highlights Tech Billionaires’ Wealth

In a separate post, Sanders broadened his criticism by highlighting the fortunes of several prominent technology executives.

"Thank you, President Trump for bringing together the Oligarchs who run our country," Sanders wrote, adding that the executives collectively hold more than $1.7 trillion in wealth.

Sanders listed Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) CEO Elon Musk at $920 billion, Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos at $368 billion, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg at $250 billion and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang at $200 billion.

Sanders contrasted those fortunes with the economic struggles of working Americans, describing the concentration of wealth as "obscene."

Trump’s AI Accord Sets Safeguards For Tech Giants

On Tuesday, Trump unveiled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, also known as the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.

The voluntary agreement includes commitments from tech leaders, including Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Zuckerberg, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Musk and Huang.

The accord calls on participating companies to implement internal safeguards and subject their AI systems to independent external reviews.

Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) has reportedly classified some of its artificial intelligence data centers as ‘pilot models’ to claim billions of dollars in federal research tax credits, potentially reducing the cost of its massive AI infrastructure push.

Meta’s AI Data Centers Under Tax Scrutiny

According to a New York Times report, Meta has described certain AI data centers to the Internal Revenue Service as "pilot models" involved in experimental work, allowing the company to claim the research and experimentation tax credit.

The tax incentive is intended to encourage companies to invest in research, including qualifying experimental projects and supplies.

Meta’s research tax credits reduced its tax bill by $3.9 billion in 2025, up from $2 billion in 2024 and $700 million in 2023, according to company filings cited by The Times.

However, the classification reportedly remains a gray area. Meta’s accountants have raised concerns that the IRS could challenge the treatment, according to people familiar with the company’s operations cited by the Times.

Meta did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment.

Read Also: Meta’s AI Spending Suddenly Makes Sense

Nvidia Chips At the Center of the Spending

The tax claims reportedly involve chips Meta purchases for its AI data centers, including Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GPUs.

Meta has significantly expanded its relationship with Nvidia, agreeing earlier this year to purchase millions of chips as it races to build AI infrastructure.

The Times also reported that Meta’s auditor, EY, has promoted the tax strategy to other AI companies.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone told the publication that the company has invested $200 billion in research and development over the past five years, including $57 billion in the last year.

The company uses tax incentives established by Congress to support domestic investment in research, technology and jobs, Stone stated.

AI Spending Raises Bigger Financial Questions

Meta’s enormous AI investments are already weighing on its finances. The company reported quarterly free cash flow of just $784 million, roughly $8 billion below the year-ago period.

Meta is among several major technology companies, including Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

Investors such as Michael Burry have warned that the spending could become problematic if AI demand fails to justify the massive investments.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis took a dig at Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang for referring to data centers as “superintelligence factories”

In a post on Wednesday, the Governor said, “Superintelligence factories = surveillance centers.”

Read Also: Ro Khanna Takes Aim at Trump's AI Data Center Push — Wants Congress to Block Projects in Residential Communities and Cut Off Flock Camera Funding

DeSantis Challenges Flock Surveillance Use

The Governor’s comment comes amid his ongoing opposition to the use of Flock cameras. In September, Florida officials ordered local police to remove automated license plate readers from state roads, limiting the use of technology provided by private surveillance firms such as Flock Safety, the deadline for which was Wednesday, Fox Business reported.

DeSantis raised concerns about data collection, potential misuse, and the lack of oversight, warning against the growth of a "digital AI surveillance state."

A hardware and software analysis of Flock surveillance cameras found that the system can capture dozens of images per vehicle encounter. The cameras transmit data via cellular networks, while license plate and vehicle analysis appears to occur on Flock’s servers rather than on the cameras.

President Donald Trump backed the use of Flock cameras and told reporters, “I sort of like ’em because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement.”

The Rebranding of AI

DeSantis’ post also comes in the wake of Huang’s statement that data centers are evolving into “superintelligence factories.”

“We call them data centers because that’s where we hold data. But the things that we’re building now, these are really super intelligence factories. And the reason why it’s a factory is because you’re producing something of economic value,” Huang said during a panel discussion alongside Elon Musk at the launch of the America.gov portal earlier this week.

On Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the terms "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" with "Super Intelligence" or "SI" in official communications, policy documents and other non-statutory materials. Trump also released the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, which calls for independent audits, stronger internal controls and board oversight of advanced AI systems.

The pact was signed by Trump and leading technology executives, including Huang, Anthropic‘s CEO Dario Amodei, and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.‘s (NASDAQ: SPCX) CEO Elon Musk.

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) remains a key beneficiary of AI-driven memory demand as investors weigh strong earnings momentum against questions about pricing power, future supply, and the durability of the current cycle.

Micron beat earnings and raised revenue and EPS guidance, keeping the AI-driven memory demand story intact even as analysts and CNBC’s “Fast Money” traders debated whether the stock’s extraordinary run leaves room for another major leg higher.

The stock gained almost 300% year-to-date, driven by an AI-driven boom in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips required to power NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) accelerators. The company hit a $1 trillion market capitalization for the first time on May 26, 2026.

Wedbush Sees AI Demand Keeping Memory Tight

Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson focused on Micron’s earnings guidance of more than $38 per share, which he said sits near the middle of the $36-to-$40 range he had heard from buy-side investors.

Bryson told CNBC on Thursday that his memory pricing checks continue to show increases, although at a slower pace. He said the reason behind Micron’s margin trajectory matters, particularly if greater high-bandwidth memory shipments supporting AI influence profitability.

He expects additional memory supply to arrive in late 2027 and 2028, noting that increasing supply historically ends memory cycles.

However, Bryson questioned whether supply can catch demand as AI accelerator and CPU deployments expand rapidly while memory capacity grows more slowly.

“So as long as you have this strength in AI, um, even if you get more supply coming on, it’s really unclear to me that supply catches demand,” Bryson said.

He also expects Micron to favor share buybacks after restrictions tied to its CHIPS Act funding expire on Dec. 9, given the cash the company has accumulated.

Fast Money Traders Focus on Margins and Expectations

CNBC’s Fast Money trader Tim Seymour called the quarter good but said investors should focus more heavily on Micron’s margin profile than its previous data-center growth rates.

He pointed to pricing and longer-term contracts as important factors but warned that the memory story could face turbulence as additional competitors expand supply.

“I’m not chasing Micron here, but there was nothing wrong with this print,” Seymour said.

Steve Grasso, another trader, turned more constructive on Micron because expanding AI-agent use should increase inference workloads and memory demand.

“I think it could actually go higher, because agents create token demand. Tokens are inference, and inference runs on memory,” Grasso said.

Nathan Questions Size of Future Earnings Beats

Trader Dan Nathan took a more cautious view, arguing that Micron’s biggest earnings surprises may already be behind it.

He noted that the latest quarter beat consensus earnings and sales estimates by roughly 5%-6%, while current-quarter guidance was about 8% above expectations. That contrasts with the much larger surprises that helped drive Micron’s earlier rally.

Nathan said investors could increasingly price in best-case outcomes, which may explain the stock’s muted after-hours reaction.

Trader Guy Adami also highlighted Micron’s roughly 86% margins and supportive AI spending trends but cautioned that competition will eventually increase.

He pointed to the limited stock reaction despite options markets pricing in a roughly 7%-8% earnings move, suggesting investors may already have incorporated substantial optimism into the shares.

“The Big Short” investor Michael Burry is warning against industry spending of about $1 trillion on artificial intelligence, comparing the focus on large language models to a 19th-century bubble.

Using an 1880 newspaper case study, Burry argues that tech capital expenditure is misdirected, favoring the “System 2” architectures from Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Google’s parent Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) over text-predicting models.

Thought Before Language

Burry based his critique on an 1880 New York Times edition detailing a Smithsonian Institution case study titled “Thought Without Language.” The study observed Melville Ballard, a deaf-mute child who developed complex existential inquiries regarding the origins of the universe before acquiring written or sign language.

The account described Ballard communicating abstract ideas through gestures and expressions before acquiring conventional language, which Burry uses as evidence for his argument that reasoning can precede language.

Applying this physiological reality to artificial intelligence, Burry asserts that large language models are “built backward” because they attempt to scale language into reason. This method results in a primitive simulation highly prone to hallucination. According to Burry, language should be the output of understanding, not its core engine.

Read Also: Michael Burry Says Markets Should 'Tank Hard' to Stop OpenAI, Anthropic From IPOs ‘For the Benefit of Humanity’

A ‘Parameter Trap’ and Speculative Gluttony

Pointing to a second article on the same 1880 newspaper page about San Francisco “bonanza speculators” who triggered absurd market valuations in a quest for immediate fortune, Burry draws a parallel to Silicon Valley’s AI hardware frenzy.

He characterizes the current market environment as a “parameter trap” defined by “supply-side gluttony and massive capital misallocation.”

Burry warns against the “singularity” myth of scaling models in an “infinite mirror.” He views this trajectory as a directionless waste of computing resources that is completely disconnected from economic reality.

The Shift to ‘System 2’ Reasoning

Rather than abandoning AI, Burry points to reasoning-oriented approaches as a potential alternative to scaling conventional language models.

Burry points instead toward reasoning-oriented AI research, highlighting Google’s AlphaGeometry and Meta’s Coconut. AlphaGeometry combines neural and symbolic reasoning, while Coconut explores reasoning in a continuous latent space rather than relying entirely on natural-language intermediate steps.

These architectures emphasize compression and logic over brute-force text prediction, aligning with the 145-year-old revelation that true comprehension transcends language entirely.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) is expanding beyond traditional chipmaking as it builds a broader AI ecosystem around processors, software, models and systems, while experts point to agentic AI and inference as new demand drivers for its CPUs and GPUs.

AMD stock gained almost 30% in September and almost 200% year-to-date, briefly pushing the company above a $1 trillion market value, fueled by artificial intelligence infrastructure demand.

Why AMD Is Spending $8.2 Billion On World Labs

AMD agreed to acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in stock, gaining spatial-intelligence technology that can generate, reconstruct and simulate 3D environments for robotics, autonomous systems, simulation and other physical AI applications.

CEO Lisa Su said closer access to frontier-model research could help AMD anticipate future computing requirements and design its hardware, software and systems around them.

“The more you understand end to end, the better system you are going to build,” Su said. “That’s why we are acquiring World Labs.”

World Labs founder Fei-Fei Li will become AMD executive vice president and chief scientist. Li said the combination could “accelerate the flywheel between software and hardware development.”

The acquisition extends AMD’s broader AI expansion. The company previously acquired ZT Systems for $4.9 billion and Silo AI for $665 million, while also announcing a deal for specialized chip company Taalas.

AMD has also deepened ties with major AI customers. Its chip agreements with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and OpenAI included potential equity arrangements, while AMD agreed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which committed to buying tens of billions of dollars of AMD data-center chips.

Cramer Sees Agentic AI Supporting Demand

CNBC’s Jim Cramer said the shift from AI training toward inference and AI agents could create another growth engine for AMD because those workloads require more CPU processing.

Cramer called AMD’s rise under Su an “incredible run” and said he sees no sign that it is going to stop anytime soon.

He still views NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) as the leading AI-chip supplier but believes demand can support multiple vendors and said AMD’s products are more competitive than some investors recognize.

The company is also expanding its GPU business through large commitments from Meta and OpenAI, strengthening its position as AI spending broadens across CPUs, accelerators and complete computing systems.

AMD Stock Analysis

AMD stock rose more than 1% in Thursday premarket trading as investors continued to favor large-cap semiconductor stocks. Nasdaq futures gained 0.37%, while S&P 500 futures rose 0.11% before the opening bell.

The stock is benefiting from a firmer broader market and continued strength in semiconductor stocks.

AMD remains in a strong uptrend, trading well above its major moving averages. The stock is 12.1% above its 20-day SMA and 66.3% above its 200-day SMA.

Momentum is also positive, with MACD above its signal line. The stock was trading at $620.30, close to its 52-week high of $639. A breakout above that level could signal further upside, while support sits near $498.

Analyst Outlook

AMD trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 156.1, reflecting a premium valuation. Analysts have a Buy consensus rating on the stock, with an average price forecast of $618.84.

StoneX maintained a Buy rating and a $685 price forecast on Sept. 29. Rosenblatt maintained a Buy rating and a $700 price forecast the same day. Bank of America Securities maintained its Buy rating on Sept. 25 and raised its price forecast to $720.

AMD Top ETF Exposure

The stock is a major holding in several semiconductor and technology ETFs.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) has an 8.74% weighting in AMD. The Invesco AI and Next Gen Software ETF (NYSE:IGPT) has an 8.51% weighting, while the First Trust Nasdaq Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:FTXL) has a 6.79% weighting.

AMD’s sizable weight in these funds means large ETF inflows or outflows can also contribute to buying or selling pressure in the stock.

Shares of Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) climbed 1.86% to trade at $139.85 during the pre-market trading session on Thursday amid a report that Tencent Holdings Ltd. (OTC:TCEHY) has signed a major lease agreement with the company.

The Chinese tech giant has agreed to a five-year lease across multiple Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia, the Financial Times reported on Thursday.

The deal will give Tencent access to approximately 100,000 advanced AI chips unavailable in China and is valued at about $7 billion, with roughly 30% payable upfront, according to the report.

These chips will be used to further enhance Tencent’s AI models and develop agentic tools, sources told the publication.

Tencent and Oracle did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Oracle, Meta Financing Methods Mirror Enron Era, Steve Eisman Says

Chinese Firms Seek Overseas AI Compute

Chinese tech companies are turning to overseas computing capacity amid limited domestic supply and tighter U.S. export controls. In December 2025, Tencent had reportedly gained access to Nvidia Corp.’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) advanced Blackwell AI chips by renting computing capacity at a Datasection-operated data center near Osaka, Japan.

The arrangement allowed Tencent to use the Nvidia B200 processors through a third-party cloud structure despite U.S. restrictions on chip sales to China.

Last week, a report indicated that China has considered allowing companies such as ByteDance and Alibaba Group Holdings (NYSE:BABA) to buy Nvidia’s high-end RTX PRO 5500 chips.

Tencent Ramps Up AI Infrastructure Spending

Tencent has ramped up infrastructure spending to strengthen its AI capabilities and is integrating AI agents across its ecosystem, particularly in WeChat, which has more than 1.4 billion users, according to FT. The company has developed a suite of AI agents for productivity and enterprise use, led by its flagship WorkBuddy office agent, which has rapidly gained users and leads China’s PC-based office agent market.

The company’s second capital expenditure surged 176% year-over-year to RMB 53 billion ($7.9 billion), driven by AI infrastructure investments and prepayments for computing resources.

He notes that “October 1987 was a configuration, not a single shock,” warning that today’s primary missing component is a falling U.S. dollar coupled with rising long yields.

He highlights a growing internal divergence: “The economy is splitting in two. Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google is expanding its artificial intelligence lineup with Gemini 4 Argon, positioning the new frontier model to drive enterprise adoption, strengthen its agent strategy and compete more directly with OpenAI, xAI and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).

The stock gained since Wednesday, when it launched its latest offering.

Google employees spent weeks testing versions of Argon without usage caps before its restricted rollout, according to Gemini product chief Tulsee Doshi.

Google Targets Coding, Cybersecurity And Enterprise Workloads

Google told CNBC on Thursday that Gemini 4 Argon improves significantly in coding and cybersecurity and outperforms rival models in software-engineering tests.

The model ties OpenAI and xAI for first place in cybersecurity testing and leads in tasks including financial analysis and legal research, according to the company.

Argon is undergoing U.S. government safety testing, with initial access limited to cybersecurity defenders and enterprise cloud customers.

Google plans to provide updates on wider availability in the coming days. It intends to offer Argon to enterprise customers through its API and expand the model into consumer products over the coming months.

Despite positioning Argon as its top frontier model, Google plans to charge $2 per million input tokens, only slightly more than its lighter models.

Argon Could Strengthen Google’s Agent Push

The launch comes as the AI industry shifts attention from simply developing increasingly capable frontier models toward using models to power agents that can perform tasks for users.

Google already offers Spark, an AI agent currently limited to paying customers. Doshi said Argon will become part of Google’s work around Spark, potentially giving the company a stronger foundation for its agent products.

Google also enters the agent race with an existing advantage: users can already grant its services access to products such as Gmail and Calendar, giving the company an established ecosystem for integrating agent capabilities.

Meta Raises Competitive Pressure

The rollout comes as Meta gains traction with Muse, its personal AI agent, intensifying pressure on Google to turn its AI technology into products that can attract paying users.

CNBC noted that Google has yet to experience the same breakout moment in consumer agents despite its existing ecosystem.

Argon gives Google another route to unlock value from Gemini through enterprise API usage, cybersecurity applications, consumer products and a potentially broader Spark rollout, while keeping pricing close to its lighter AI models.

Several top AI leaders, including Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, reportedly confronted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, privately, regarding his public warnings about the potential dangers of AI, according to a report.

On Tuesday, the executives, after agreeing to a set of principles to ensure the safety of AI models, questioned Amodei about the severity of his public statements on the capabilities and risks of AI models, The Wall Street Journal reported. The discussion took place following President Donald Trump‘s luncheon with approximately two dozen tech CEOs in the East Room.

The Anthropic CEO urged executives to be transparent and honest about AI model capabilities and avoid downplaying potential risks, the report added.

When Amodei raised safety concerns during lunch and emphasized the importance of transparency with the public about AI model capabilities and risks, Mark Zuckerberg, the CEO of Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), suggested that the best way to address these concerns was by upholding the agreed principles as an industry, the report noted.

Amodei, who had recently dined with Trump for their first face-to-face meeting, expressed optimism about the industry’s ability to ensure safety if it collaborates with the administration.

Anthropic, Nvidia, and Meta did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Trump Says Communities Hosting AI Data Centers Could Get a ‘Dividend' From Teacher Bonuses to Payments: 'People are Going to Benefit Directly'

Anthropic Faces Scrutiny Over AI Warnings

Anthropic reported a $42 billion net loss in its IPO prospectus, prompting Porter and Company analyst Ross Hendricks to argue that the AI firm’s warnings about existential risks could be aimed at encouraging government action against cheaper open-source competitors. Hendricks highlighted that the company’s loss occurred before Anthropic "started losing market share to dirt cheap open source models."

Hendricks questioned Anthropic’s motives for highlighting AI risks to regulators, asking, "Anyone still wondering why the company is threatening to end humanity unless the government shuts down their competition?"

Previously, Jensen Huang criticized AI lab leaders for what he called "too much drama" around calls for greater AI oversight. He questioned their motives, argued that existing laws are sufficient to address safety concerns, and warned that slowing U.S. AI development could give China an advantage. Huang also rejected AI doomsday predictions as unscientific and suggested that these leaders may have “ulterior” or “political” motives.

Michael Burry is changing the way he is betting against the AI boom, shifting from outright short positions to long-dated put options. At the center of the strategy is the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), putting the broader chip industry under scrutiny as investors debate whether massive AI infrastructure spending can continue to justify semiconductor valuations.

Burry recently covered his SOXX short and replaced it with September 2027 puts struck in the low $400s. He made similar moves in Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA), Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU), Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR),
Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS), and Oracle Corp (NYSE:ORCL), saying, on a Substack post, that he has become more confident that the AI bubble could burst "sooner than later."

Read Also: Michael Burry, Peter Schiff Flag S&P 500 Risk: 5 ETFs to Consider Now

SOXX’s Q3 Pullback Puts the Debate In Focus

The timing is notable. SOXX fell 11% in the third quarter, its weakest quarterly performance since March 2025.

Yet the semiconductor story remains closely tied to real AI demand. SOXX, which holds 30 companies, has about $48.4 billion in assets and traded at a trailing P/E of nearly 68. Semiconductors account for 82.3% of the portfolio, with another 17.6% in semiconductor equipment.

That exposure makes SOXX a useful gauge of the broader economics of the AI buildout. Burry’s argument is that increasingly powerful models could eventually require less computing, challenging the assumption that more AI adoption automatically means exponentially more chips.

The Capex Machine Is Still Running

For now, spending remains enormous. S&P Global estimates that Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta Platforms, Inc (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Oracle will collectively spend about $750 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, equal to 38% of their revenue.

But the latest data offers a counterpoint to Burry’s thesis. Micron said Wednesday that customers have increased commitments under long-term supply agreements to $32 billion, while the company has secured most of its 2027 HBM output. Data-center SSD revenue also nearly topped $10 billion in fiscal Q4, more than 10 times the year-ago level. Micron said larger AI models, longer context windows and higher user concurrency are driving greater memory and storage requirements.

For now, the data is pulling in two directions. Burry is betting that more efficient AI could eventually undermine the massive hardware buildout, while Micron’s latest results show customers locking in billions of dollars of memory capacity as AI workloads continue to expand. That puts SOXX at the center of a bigger debate: whether AI efficiency will ultimately reduce chip demand or simply make room for the next wave of AI applications.

September is usually the worst month of the year for chip stocks. This year, it was one of the best.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) rose 11.3% in September 2026, its second-best September since 2001.

Only September 2010 was stronger, with a 14.9% gain.

The calendar now turns in the sector’s favor.

Over the past 25 years, the five months from October to February have been the best stretch of the year to own semiconductor stocks.

October To February Is The Best Window To Own Chip Stocks

SOXX enters October up 88.8% in 2026, making semiconductors the best-performing industry in the U.S. stock market this year.

From October to February, SOXX gained an average of 2.4% a month. From March to September, the average was 0.7% a month.

In other words, the ETF has earned close to four times more per month in the colder half of the calendar.

Measured as a full season, the October-to-February window returned an average of 12.5% across 25 seasons since 2001. The median gain was 12%.

The window ended higher in 21 of those 25 seasons. That is a success rate of 84%.

The most recent season, from October 2025 to February 2026, delivered a 29.9% gain.

November stands out within the window. SOXX has gained an average of 5.2% in November, the highest of any calendar month.

The ETF rose in 19 of 25 Novembers, or 76% of the time. Only May matches that hit rate, with a lower average gain of 4.9%.

Some Novembers were exceptional. SOXX jumped 23.8% in November 2002, 18.9% in November 2022 and 18.4% in November 2020.

Bank of America Names Its Top Chip Picks For The Season

Bank of America sees the same pattern.

In a note shared Tuesday, analyst Vivek Arya said the fourth and first calendar quarters have been the two best seasons to own chip stocks.

From 2010 to 2025, chip stocks delivered “300-500bps of median outperformance vs. SPX” in those quarters, he said. In other words, they beat the S&P 500 by a median of 3 to 5 percentage points.

Arya named five top picks with near-term catalysts.

They are Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC), Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), Marvell Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL) and Lam Research Corp. (NASDAQ:LRCX).

For Nvidia, the catalysts are larger buybacks and several GTC developer conferences.

For Intel, it is rising demand for its processors in AI agents and a possible customer win for its contract manufacturing business.

Micron is set to start buybacks in December. Marvell holds its Analyst Day on Oct. 6, while Lam Research could gain market share in equipment for both memory and logic chips.

Shares of Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU) slipped 1.9% in early trading on Thursday, even after the company reported record fiscal fourth-quarter results and guided well above expectations.

• Micron stock is moving today. What’s going on?

Here are some key analyst takeaways:

  • Rosenblatt analyst Kevin Cassidy reiterated a Buy rating, while raising the price target from $1,500 to $1,900.
  • D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria reiterated a Buy rating, while raising the price target from $2,000 to $2,100.
  • J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur reiterated an Overweight rating and price target of $1,540.
  • Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse reiterated an Overweight rating and price target of $2,000.
  • Needham analyst N. Quinn Bolton reaffirmed a Buy rating and price target of $1,650.
  • Bank of America Securities analyst Vivek Arya reiterated a Buy rating and price target of $1,550.
  • RBC Capital Markets analyst Srini Pajjuri reiterated an Outperform rating and price target of $1,500.

Check out other analyst stock ratings.

Micron Analyst Commentary

Rosenblatt: “We were surprised by management’s outlook for a deceleration of DRAM bit growth Y/Y,” Cassidy said in a note. Industry growth in DRAM, the main memory used in servers, PCs and phones, should slow to the low-20% range in 2027 and 2028 from the mid-20% range in 2026, as high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is harder to make.

Faster cleanroom construction lifts fiscal 2027 capital spending above $50 billion, versus Rosenblatt’s prior $45 billion forecast. Even so, Cassidy expects free cash flow above $100 billion. His target is 10 times his fiscal 2028 earnings estimate of $190 per share.

D.A. Davidson: Management signaled that memory markets could be even tighter in 2028 than today, Luria said, “addressing a key investor concern that current fundamentals represent a cyclical peak.”

Boise, Idaho-based Micron now has 26 strategic customer agreements (SCAs), up 10 from a quarter ago. Even at floor prices, gross margins should stay above the prior cycle peak of 61%, the analyst noted. His target is 13 times calendar 2027 earnings.

J.P. Morgan: More than 75% of fiscal 2027 output is already committed across customers, which Sur called “an unprecedented level of forward visibility.”

New SCAs are being priced at today’s elevated market levels, which in his view sets a higher and more durable margin floor.

Sur estimates about $108 billion in free cash flow from the second through fourth quarters of fiscal 2027. He expects buybacks at scale right after Dec. 9, with management already signaling a request for a larger repurchase authorization.

Cantor Fitzgerald: Muse said he could not recall a management team ever guiding for revenue and gross margin to grow every quarter for a full year.

Cantor models over $333 billion in free cash flow over the next eight quarters, with aggressive buybacks starting Dec. 9, when CHIPS Act limits end.

At about 5.6 times Muse’s calendar 2027 earnings estimate of $188 per share, Micron is “simply too cheap to ignore,” he wrote.

Needham: “Execution on HBM is continuing as gross margins are approaching DRAM margin levels,” Bolton said.

The vast majority of calendar 2027 HBM supply is already contracted at significantly higher prices. Needham estimates quarterly HBM revenue at about $6.0 billion, up from $5.2 billion. Customer commitments under the SCAs rose to $32 billion, mostly cash deposits.

Bank of America Securities: Arya raised his fiscal 2027 and 2028 earnings estimates by 23% and 36%, to $172 and $198 per share. As memory claims a bigger share of AI spending, “we expect memory to increasingly capture more value in 2027 and beyond,” he wrote.

He sees upside to Wall Street’s $30 billion to $35 billion fiscal 2027 buyback estimate, with repurchases reaching $60 billion to $100 billion a year by fiscal 2028 and 2029. The risks he flagged are an unclear near-term buyback level, customers designing in less HBM and competition from China’s CXMT.

RBC Capital Markets: Results and guidance came in slightly ahead of expectations, Pajjuri said, as he lifted his fiscal 2027 earnings estimate to $162.91 from $145.78.

At about 6.5 times that figure, valuation is “barely giving credit to floor pricing agreements,” he wrote. SCAs remain untested in a downturn, but should offer meaningful protection even if some customers fall short.

Price Action

Micron shares had fallen 1.92% to $1,044.71 at the time of publication on Thursday.
